title: Decorator — add toppings to pizza, add features to a base product.

s1_definition.profdef: The Decorator pattern attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in a decorator that implements the same interface and delegates to the wrapped object while adding behaviour. It provides a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the Decorator as adding optional features onto a base bank account at National Bank of India. Rajesh starts with a basic account; he wraps it with overdraft protection, then wraps that with premium rewards. s1_definition.oneliner: The Decorator pattern wraps an object to add behaviour dynamically, stacking features without an explosion of subclasses.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Decorator pattern attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in a decorator that implements the same interface and delegates to the wrapped object while adding behaviour. It provides a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the Decorator as adding optional features onto a base bank account at National Bank of India. Rajesh starts with a basic account; he wraps it with overdraft protection, then wraps that with premium rewards. Each wrapper adds its own fee or benefit on top of whatever it wraps, so you can stack features in any combination without creating a separate class for every possible mix.

**One line to remember:** The Decorator pattern wraps an object to add behaviour dynamically, stacking features without an explosion of subclasses.

sections.s2_technical:
Both the base component and the decorators implement the same interface, which is what lets a decorated object be used anywhere the original was expected. A decorator holds a reference to a component, delegates the core call to it, and adds its own contribution before or after.

```java
AccountFeature acc = new RewardsFeature(new OverdraftFeature(new BasicAccount()));
BigDecimal fee = acc.monthlyFee();
```

The strength over subclassing is combinatorial. If a product has three optional features, subclassing would need a class for every combination, but decorators let you compose any subset at runtime by stacking wrappers. This satisfies Open/Closed, because a new feature is a new decorator, and the Single Responsibility principle, because each decorator does one thing.

The senior nuance is ordering and transparency: because each decorator wraps the same interface, callers remain unaware of the stack, but the order can matter when one decorator's output feeds another. I keep decorators commutative where possible and document the order where it is significant, and I avoid overly deep stacks that hurt readability.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India offers a basic account with optional add-ons like overdraft and rewards, and customers want any combination. Creating a class for every combination is unmanageable. This is exactly the Decorator pattern composing features.

Problem 2 — The bank launches a new "insurance" add-on, and existing account code must not change. This is exactly the Open/Closed benefit of adding a decorator.

The code defines an `AccountFeature` interface, a base account, and fee decorators, with a demo computing Rajesh's monthly fee for a stacked account.
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.decorator.DecoratorDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh's account built as rewards wrapping overdraft wrapping a basic account.

Step 1: a BasicAccount is created with a base fee of 100. Step 2: it is wrapped by an OverdraftFeature, which will add 50 to whatever it wraps. Step 3: that is wrapped by a RewardsFeature, which will add 75. Step 4: calling `monthlyFee` on the outer rewards decorator delegates inward: rewards asks overdraft, overdraft asks basic which returns 100, overdraft adds 50 for 150, rewards adds 75 for 225. The description assembles the same way.

```
Oct 31 22:24 INFO ACC: Basic + Overdraft + Rewards monthly fee = 225
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Decorator ═══

  ┌─ Pattern ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Decorator: FeatureDecorator wraps AccountFeature  │
  │   WHY: compose features, avoid subclass explosion │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: each decorator adds one feature                │
  │ O: new feature = new decorator                    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ <<interface>>    │
  │ AccountFeature   │
  │ + monthlyFee()   │
  └────────┬─────────┘
      ┌────┴───────────────┐
      ▼                    ▼
  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ BasicAccount │  │ FeatureDecorator │◆── wraps AccountFeature
  │ (component)  │  │ (abstract)       │
  └──────────────┘  └────────┬─────────┘
                       ┌─────┴──────┐
                       ▼            ▼
                 OverdraftFeature  RewardsFeature

  Call Chain:
  1. Rewards.monthlyFee → Overdraft.monthlyFee → Basic (100)
  2. +50 → 150 → +75 → 225
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Decorator pattern attaches extra responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in a decorator that implements the same interface, delegates to the wrapped object, and adds its own behaviour. It is the flexible alternative to subclassing, and I reach for it whenever a base thing has many optional features that customers want to combine freely.

The structure is a shared interface implemented by both the base component and the decorators. Each decorator holds a reference to a component, delegates the core call to it, and contributes its own part before or after. Because the decorator implements the same interface, a decorated object can be used anywhere the original was expected, so the caller never needs to know how deep the stack goes.

The decisive advantage over subclassing is combinatorial. If a product has several optional features, subclassing would require a separate class for every possible combination, which explodes quickly, whereas decorators let me compose any subset at runtime by stacking wrappers. This satisfies the Open/Closed principle, because a new feature is a new decorator, and the Single Responsibility principle, because each decorator does exactly one thing.

The senior nuance I keep in mind is ordering. Because each decorator wraps the same interface, callers stay unaware of the stack, but the order can matter when one decorator's output feeds the next, so I keep decorators commutative where I can and document the order where it is significant. In my banking work at National Bank of India, I model optional account add-ons like overdraft, rewards, and insurance as decorators, so a customer can mix and match features and the monthly fee composes automatically, without the bank ever maintaining a class for every combination.
